parts.title: Argovit™ Silver Nanoparticles Reduce the Damage That Sodium Arsenite Does to the DNA and Division of Human Lymphocytes Grown in the Lab
parts.abstract: Arsenic is a poison that can harm the DNA inside our cells, and people can be exposed to it in the environment or at work. This puts their health at serious risk, so it is important to find substances that can reduce the harm it causes. In this study, we tested whether Argovit™, a product made of extremely tiny silver particles called silver nanoparticles, could protect human lymphocytes from damage caused by sodium arsenite. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that help fight infection. We grew them in the lab from whole blood taken from healthy donors, so the cells were outside the body. We exposed the lymphocytes to sodium arsenite (3.7 × 10−3 µg/mL) and to Argovit™ silver nanoparticles (3.6 × 10−3 µg/mL). To look for damage, we used a standard test called the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) test. We changed it so that it ran for 144 hours instead of the usual time, which let us see delayed effects across two full rounds of cell division. We compared four groups: untreated cells, cells given sodium arsenite only, cells given silver nanoparticles only, and cells given sodium arsenite and then silver nanoparticles. Sodium arsenite increased the signs of damage to cells and to their DNA. In contrast, giving the silver nanoparticles afterwards significantly reduced these effects. We ran every treatment twice, and we compared the groups with a statistical method called the Kruskal–Wallis test, followed by Dunn's test to compare pairs of groups. We called a result statistically significant when p < 0.05, meaning that if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time. Our statistical analysis confirmed that Argovit™ protects cells and their DNA. These findings support the idea that it could be used to reduce harm when people are exposed to DNA-damaging substances in the environment or at work.
parts.introduction_first: Over the past few decades, scientists have paid a lot of attention to silver nanoparticles, which are tiny particles of silver, far too small to see. They have drawn interest because they can fight germs and cancer, and because they might be useful in gene therapy, a way of treating disease by changing or repairing genes [1,2]. Silver nanoparticles have special properties that let them interact with cells and with the molecules inside them. This has opened the door to using them to reduce the DNA damage caused by harmful substances in the environment and in chemicals [3,4,5,6]. One of these harmful substances is sodium arsenite, a pollutant in the environment that has been studied a great deal because of the harm it does to human health. It mainly causes damage to DNA and to cells of many different kinds [7,8]. Among the silver nanoparticle products, Argovit™ has been studied widely because it is very good at fighting germs and could be useful in medicine [9,10,11]. Russian researchers developed Argovit™. Its silver particles are wrapped in a protective coating of a substance called polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). This coating makes the particles more stable and less toxic than other silver nanoparticles [12]. It also lets scientists control more precisely how the particles interact with cells and tissues, which makes them especially attractive for early studies done before testing in people [12,13]. Silver nanoparticles have been shown to act as antioxidants, meaning they help protect cells from oxidative stress, a kind of chemical wear and tear that can damage DNA. Even so, scientists still disagree about whether they cause damage to cells and DNA [14]. Several studies have tested Argovit™ in cells grown in the lab. They found that, at low amounts, it can reduce DNA damage, but at high amounts it can cause damage to cells and DNA in different types of cells [2,11,15]. The results depend on the conditions of the experiment and on the type of cell used. This shows why more research is needed on how safe these particles are, and how they work, in particular situations, such as when they meet DNA-damaging substances like sodium arsenite [10,16,17].
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

Our study suggests that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles may partly protect human lymphocytes grown in the lab from the damage that sodium arsenite does to cells and their DNA. When we gave the silver nanoparticles after the arsenite exposure, we saw a significant recovery in the nuclear division index (NDI), a measure of how many nuclei the cells had formed. We also saw fewer signs of DNA damage, including micronuclei (MNi), which are small extra nuclei that hold loose pieces of DNA; nucleoplasmic bridges (NPBs), which are abnormal strands linking two nuclei; and nuclear buds (NBuds), which are small outgrowths from a nucleus. These findings point to a possible reduction in damage to chromosomes, the packages that hold our DNA, and to a relative improvement in how the cells multiply. However, more evidence is needed to show how large this protective effect is and exactly what it protects against.

We changed the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) test so that it ran for a longer time, 144 hours. This let us measure DNA damage that builds up over time and shows up later, and it let us look at whether the silver nanoparticles could help repair it. Extending the test in this way is a useful step forward in studying how nanoparticles and DNA-damaging substances interact, because it gives us a longer window, covering two full rounds of cell division.

The effects we saw may come from several processes. The particles may act as antioxidants, using glutathione, a natural substance in cells that neutralizes harmful oxygen-based molecules. They may reduce oxidative stress, change the way cells respond to DNA damage, and form a biocorona, a layer of proteins that gathers around the particles. This layer may help the particles reach the cells more easily while keeping down unwanted reactions. However, we did not measure direct signs of programmed cell death (apoptosis), of cells stopping their division, or of DNA repair. This limits how firm we can be about how the protection works.

Future studies should measure changes over time at several points, look for signs of programmed cell death and oxidative stress, and study the physical and chemical properties of the particles to see how arsenite and silver nanoparticles might interact. In addition, studies that expose cells to both substances over a long time will be essential. They will help us judge the risk of DNA damage when people are exposed to nanoparticles and chemical pollutants in the environment or at work for many years.
parts.introduction_rest:
Arsenic is a metalloid, an element that behaves partly like a metal and partly like a non-metal. It occurs naturally all around us, in many different chemical forms. One of the most poisonous of these is sodium arsenite. The U.S. Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) ranks arsenic first on its list of the 10 most hazardous substances. It does so because arsenic is known to cause mutations (changes in DNA), cancer, and birth defects [18]. Many studies have recorded these effects, both in experiments and in studies of large groups of people. They show that being exposed to arsenic for a long time, even at low levels, can lead to several kinds of cancer, such as skin, lung, bladder and kidney cancer [18,19].

Sodium arsenite dissolves in water. It can quickly get into the human body when people drink contaminated water, breathe it in, or touch it with their skin, and it then directly affects how cells work. One of the main things arsenic can do is damage DNA. It can break the strands of DNA, cause abnormal chromosomes, and make micronuclei (small extra nuclei) form in exposed cells. These changes are signs of damage to DNA. This kind of damage comes before mutations and before cancer develops [18,20].

Sodium arsenite harms both cells and their DNA, and it affects many types of cells. These include human lymphocytes, which play a key part in the immune system. Lymphocytes help defend the body against invaders and abnormal cells, such as bacteria, viruses and cancer cells [19,21]. Inside cells, sodium arsenite produces reactive oxygen species (ROS). These are harmful, highly reactive molecules that contain oxygen. They cause oxidative stress (chemical wear and tear), change the signals that cells use to communicate, and damage the structure of DNA. This damage can show up as micronuclei, broken DNA strands and other signs that the cell's genetic material is unstable. All of these help cells change in harmful ways and help cancer develop [22,23].

Several studies have confirmed that sodium arsenite is a strong cause of mutations and can cause birth defects, affecting how embryos develop in living things exposed to it. Arsenic also harms cells in other ways. It can trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death) and necrosis (a more chaotic kind of cell death), and it can stop mitochondria, the cell's power stations, from working properly. All of this makes it harder for cells to stay alive. In experiments, long exposure to this substance has clearly been linked to cells multiplying less and to more signs of programmed cell death [19,24,25,26].

Silver nanoparticles have been shown to act as antioxidants [27], and they protect cells from damage, especially from the reactive oxygen species that poisonous substances produce [28,29]. Several studies have shown that silver nanoparticles can interfere with the processes that produce these harmful molecules. This lowers oxidative stress in cells and, as a result, DNA damage [15]. However, we still do not fully understand how silver nanoparticles interact with poisonous substances such as sodium arsenite. Recent studies suggest that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles may protect cells when they are given after exposure to DNA-damaging substances. This makes them a possible option for use in medicine to prevent genetic damage.

The cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) test has been widely used to measure damage to DNA in human and animal cells [30]. It works especially well for spotting damage to chromosomes or to the process of cell division that leads to micronuclei forming in cells with two nuclei [31]. The test is usually run for 72 hours. However, recent studies have tried changing the method [32], for example by changing how long the cells are kept with the substances. This may make it easier to see damage to DNA at later stages of cell division or under particular experimental conditions [33]. In our study, we changed the test to run for 144 hours. This gave us a chance to look at the long-term effects of Argovit™ silver nanoparticles after exposure to sodium arsenite, and to find out how these particles may help reduce damage to DNA.

Most studies on how silver nanoparticles and arsenic interact have focused on technology. For example, researchers have used silver nanoparticles to build nano filters that detect and remove arsenic from wastewater and from contaminated soil [34,35]. These studies have given promising results for cleaning up the environment. In that work, the particles' ability to catch substances on their surface and to fight germs plays a key role [36,37]. However, very few studies have looked at how silver nanoparticles and arsenic interact in living things, either inside the body or in cells grown in the lab. Because so little research has been done here, there is a big gap in what we know about the biological effects of this interaction, especially whether it harms cells and DNA in human cells. This lack of research shows that we need to study the health effects of silver nanoparticles further, particularly when they are combined with DNA-damaging substances such as sodium arsenite.

So far, only a few studies have looked at how silver nanoparticles and sodium arsenite interact in cells grown in the lab [38,39]. Some early work has shown that silver nanoparticles can partly cancel out the damage caused by heavy metals and other poisonous substances. They do this by lowering oxidative stress and by helping the cell's DNA repair systems work better [21,39].

Silver nanoparticles have become promising candidates for finding substances that could reduce the DNA damage caused by arsenite, because of their special physical, chemical and biological properties [38]. Among them, Argovit™ silver nanoparticles stand out because their safety is well documented and because they have been shown to protect in many different biological tests. Earlier safety tests, carried out following OECD Guideline 420 (an international standard method for testing how poisonous a substance is when swallowed), found that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles have low acute oral toxicity, meaning they cause little harm when swallowed in a single dose. Their LD50 values, the amount needed to kill half of the test animals, place them in Category 4 of the Globally Harmonized System, the international system for classifying how poisonous chemicals are [40]. Studies in mice exposed to the cancer drugs cytosine arabinoside and cyclophosphamide found no significant damage. Instead, the particles had no effect on DNA and even protected it [41,42]. Studies in the environment have also shown that the particles cause little harm to plant cells [43]. In addition, Argovit™ has been well tolerated by human red blood cells and lymphocytes [10,41,42]. It has also been used successfully in medical care, including to prevent SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19), to treat diabetic foot ulcers, and in breathing care [44]. All of these features make Argovit™ a particularly good choice for testing whether it can reduce the damage that arsenite does to cells and their DNA in human lymphocytes [45].

With this in mind, it is important to find out whether giving silver nanoparticles after exposure to sodium arsenite can reduce the harm it does to cells and their DNA, especially in human lymphocytes. In this work, we aim to help explain how Argovit™ silver nanoparticles protect cells when they are given after exposure to a DNA-damaging substance such as sodium arsenite [35,36,37,38]. Using a changed version of the cytokinesis-block micronucleus test, we aim to learn more about how silver nanoparticles might reduce cell damage, and about whether they could be used in preventive medical treatments for people exposed to DNA-damaging substances in the environment or at work. Our hypothesis, the idea we set out to test, is that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles reduce the damage that sodium arsenite does to cells and their DNA in human lymphocytes when they are given after the arsenite exposure. Our goal is to measure how much Argovit™ silver nanoparticles reduce the harm that sodium arsenite does to cells and their DNA in human lymphocytes, using the changed cytokinesis-block micronucleus test run for 144 hours.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Preparing the Argovit™ Silver Nanoparticles and Checking Their Properties

The silver nanoparticles we used came from Argovit™, a product donated by Dr. Vasily Burmistrov of the Vector-Vita Scientific and Production Center in Novosibirsk, Russia. Argovit™ is a stable liquid made of water. It contains 1.2% pure silver by weight, and the silver is held in place by 18.8% polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), the protective coating. The PVP molecules have an average size of 12.6 ± 2.7 kDa. (A kDa, or kilodalton, is a unit used to describe the size of molecules.)

The physical and chemical properties of this product have already been studied in detail [46]. The particles are round, with an average diameter of 35 ± 12 nm, measured with a transmission electron microscope (TEM), a very powerful microscope that can show objects far too small for an ordinary one. When the particles float in liquid, they move around, and this movement makes them look bigger than they really are. Measured this way, their diameter is about 70 nm. We also measured their zeta potential, which tells us the electric charge on the surface of the particles. It was −15 mV, meaning the particles carry a negative charge. Finally, the particles absorb light most strongly at a wavelength of 420 nm. This is called their surface plasmon resonance peak, and it is a typical sign of silver nanoparticles [46].

We used these measurements as quality checks to make sure each batch of the product was the same throughout the experiment. The particles did not clump together or become unstable, either while they were stored or when we diluted them in the liquid used to grow the cells. Three features are thought to be critical for how well the particles get along with living cells and how they behave in the body. These are their ability to stay spread out in liquid, their negative surface charge, and their PVP coating. This matters especially for how the particles interact with the outer layer of cells, called the cell membrane, and how they get inside cells grown outside the body [46].

2.2. Preparing the Sodium Arsenite Treatment

We dissolved sodium arsenite (NaAsO2, from Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in water at a concentration of 10 mM. (mM, or millimolar, is a unit that tells how much of a substance is dissolved in a liquid.) We then diluted this solution in the liquid used to grow the cells, so that the final amount in the treatments was 3.7 × 10−3 µg/mL.

We chose this amount because, in our earlier CBMN tests, a sodium arsenite concentration of 3.7 × 103 µg/mL had been confirmed as a positive control for DNA damage. A positive control is a substance known to cause the effect we are looking for, so it shows that the test is working. This amount always caused damage to chromosomes [10]. It also falls within the range that other researchers have reported for causing micronuclei to form in human lymphocytes without killing many cells or stopping them from dividing [10].

2.3. Growing the Human Lymphocytes

The cells came from three separate samples of 0.5 mL each of whole blood taken from a vein. All the blood came from a single healthy adult donor, aged 25–35 years, who did not smoke. In the three months before the study, the donor had no known exposure to DNA-damaging substances, no medicines, and no long-lasting illnesses. We took the blood by a needle from a vein.

We followed the guidelines of the Bioethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine and Psychology at the Autonomous University of Baja California, Tijuana (approval number 05/2014-1). We added heparin to the blood to stop it from clotting. We then grew the cells directly as whole blood in RPMI-1640, a standard liquid used to grow cells in the lab. To this liquid we added 15% fetal bovine serum, a nutrient-rich liquid from calf blood, along with two antibiotics, penicillin (100 U/mL) and streptomycin (100 µg/mL).

To make the lymphocytes multiply, we added phytohemagglutinin (PHA), a plant protein that triggers lymphocytes to divide, at a final amount of 5 µg/mL. We kept the cultures at 37 °C in air containing 5% carbon dioxide.

We used whole blood instead of first separating out the lymphocytes. This kept the cells in their natural surroundings, so that substances in the plasma (the liquid part of blood) and other blood factors could shape how the cells responded. Working with cells outside the body in this way matches established methods for the CBMN test in human lymphocytes. It also makes our findings more relevant to real biology and more useful for understanding what might happen in people [47].

2.4. Changing the Liquid the Cells Grew In

After 72 hours of growth, we spun the cells in a centrifuge, a machine that spins samples very fast so that the cells collect at the bottom. We then removed 5 mL of the liquid and added fresh RPMI-1640 with PHA at five µg/mL. The cells then grew for another 72 hours, so the whole experiment lasted 144 hours from the start (Figure 1).

2.5. The CBMN Test

We carried out the CBMN test following the standard method described in [47], with one important change: we made the whole experiment last 144 hours instead of the original 72 hours.

We added the test substances, sodium arsenite, silver nanoparticles, or both, 24 hours after the start of the culture [48,49]. In the group that received both, we added the second substance, either sodium arsenite or silver nanoparticles, 72 hours after the start. At 116 hours, we added cytochalasin B (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) at a final amount of 6 µg/mL. This substance stops cytokinesis, the final step in which a cell splits into two. As a result, some cells end up with two nuclei, called binucleated cells.

After the full 144 hours, we collected the cells by spinning them in a centrifuge. We then preserved them in a mixture of methanol and acetic acid (3 parts to 1). We stained the samples with two dyes, eosin and methylene blue, which color the different parts of the cell so they are easy to see. Finally, we looked at them under a light microscope and counted the signs of damage to cells and their DNA.

Figure 2 shows typical examples of the different kinds of nuclei and damage we saw in the CBMN test. These include cells with one nucleus, two nuclei, or several nuclei, as well as cells going through programmed cell death. They also include micronuclei (MNi), nuclear buds (NBuds), and nucleoplasmic bridges (NPBs) [50].

2.6. How We Set Up the Experiment

Our experiment was based on a changed version of the CBMN test first proposed by Fenech and Morley [47]. We extended it to 144 hours so that we could look at two full rounds of cell division and catch damage that shows up later. Whitwell and colleagues (2015) support this longer method. They showed that a longer growing time, together with refreshing the liquid the cells grow in, makes the test more stable and better at picking up damage in lymphocytes from the blood [48].

As Figure 1 shows, we set up four groups. Each group used 0.5 mL of whole blood from a vein, grown outside the body for 144 hours [48]:

(1)

Control group (untreated cells): At 0 hours, we added PHA and RPMI-1640 to make the lymphocytes multiply. At 72 hours, we replaced part of the liquid with fresh RPMI containing PHA. At 116 hours, we added cytochalasin B (6 µg/mL) to stop cytokinesis, and we collected the cells at 144 hours. This group shows how the cells behave without any harmful substance or nanoparticles.

(2)

Sodium arsenite (NaAsO2) group: This group was treated exactly like the control group, except that we added sodium arsenite (3.7 × 10−3 µg/mL) at 24 hours. It serves as a positive control for DNA damage, because sodium arsenite is well known to cause damage to chromosomes in human lymphocytes.

(3)

Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) group: We added silver nanoparticles (3.6 × 10−3 µg/mL) at 24 hours, under the same conditions as the control group. We designed this group to test whether Argovit™ silver nanoparticles can cause damage to cells and their DNA on their own. We used an amount below the level that causes harm, which our group had already confirmed in earlier work [10].

(4)

Sodium arsenite + silver nanoparticles group (silver nanoparticles given after arsenite): We added PHA and RPMI-1640 at 0 hours. At 24 hours, we added sodium arsenite alone to cause damage to cells and their DNA. At 72 hours, we refreshed the liquid and added PHA and silver nanoparticles (3.6 × 10−3 µg/mL). This group was meant to find out whether giving silver nanoparticles after the arsenite exposure could reduce the damage caused by sodium arsenite. It imitates a possible treatment or recovery situation. We added cytochalasin B at 116 hours and collected the cells at 144 hours.

In all groups, we also refreshed the liquid at 96 hours and 120 hours. This kept the cells alive and gave them enough nutrients throughout the long experiment.

We ran every condition twice, following the advice in the standard CBMN test method by Fenech [47,48,49,50,51]. Running each condition twice helps make sure the test gives the same results when repeated and reduces differences between the two runs.

2.7. How We Analyzed the Results

We ran every condition twice, following the advice in the CBMN test method [51]. That method suggests using two cultures to make results from human lymphocytes more reliable and easier to repeat.

For each run, we looked at 500 cells to work out the nuclear division index (NDI) and the percentage of cells going through programmed cell death. To look for signs of DNA damage, we looked at 1000 binucleated cells. In these cells, we counted micronuclei (MNi), nucleoplasmic bridges (NPBs), and nuclear buds (NBuds).

We calculated the nuclear division index with this formula:

NDI = (M1 + 2M2 + 3M3 + 4M4) / N

Here, M1 to M4 are the numbers of cells with 1, 2, 3, and 4 nuclei, and N is the total number of living cells we looked at. In other words, we add up the nuclei in all the cells and divide by the number of cells.

The counts we measured are whole numbers, and they often follow a pattern called a Poisson distribution, which describes counts of things that happen at random. Because of this, we first used Bartlett's test to check whether the results were spread out by similar amounts in each group. They were not. So we transformed the data, meaning we changed the numbers mathematically, to make them closer to a normal distribution, the familiar bell-shaped curve.

To compare the groups, we used the Kruskal–Wallis test, followed by Dunn's test to compare pairs of groups. These are non-parametric tests, which means they do not assume the data follow a bell-shaped curve. We called a result statistically significant when p < 0.05. This means that if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

We did all the statistical analysis and made all the graphs with two computer programs: Jamovi (version 2.5) and GraphPad Prism (version 9.0).
parts.results:
3. Results

In this study, we tested how Argovit™ silver nanoparticles affect the damage that sodium arsenite does to human lymphocytes grown in the lab from blood. We looked at two kinds of harm: damage to the cells themselves and damage to their DNA. Cells given silver nanoparticles after sodium arsenite were clearly less harmed than untreated cells. We used the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) test, which looks at cells that have two nuclei. In these cells, the silver nanoparticles led to a statistically significant drop in the number of micronuclei, the small extra nuclei that hold loose pieces of DNA. Supplementary Table S1 gives the detailed results for each group, including the statistically significant differences between treatments. The figures in the sections below show these results.

3.1. Damage to the Cells

We first looked at the cell division index (Figure 3a), which measures how many nuclei the cells had formed. The untreated group (CTR) and the group given sodium arsenite (As) were significantly different. This shows that sodium arsenite has a strong effect on cell division compared with untreated cells. The other two treatments, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) alone and sodium arsenite followed by silver nanoparticles (As + AgNPs), showed no significant difference from the untreated group. This suggests that the nanoparticles may protect the cells, or at the very least do not make the harm from sodium arsenite worse. Dunn's test, which compares pairs of groups, found a significant difference between the untreated group and the sodium arsenite group (p < 0.05, marked with **).

We also looked at programmed cell death (apoptosis), the process in which a cell destroys itself in a planned way (Figure 3b). We found no significant increase in it. This suggests that sodium arsenite does its damage mainly by getting in the way of the cell's ability to divide. It may do this by damaging the DNA in a way that stops the cell from moving through its cycle of growth and division. It does not seem to directly switch on the cell's self-destruct program. Because the silver nanoparticles did not increase programmed cell death, they could be working to fight the damage without triggering it (Figure 3b).

This could matter if you are judging how safe silver nanoparticles are, or how well they protect cells. Their effect does not seem to include switching on programmed cell death, which could be a good sign when the goal is to reduce harm to cells without encouraging them to die.

3.2. Damage to the DNA

We looked at three signs of DNA damage: micronuclei (MNi), nucleoplasmic bridges (NPBs) and nuclear buds (NBuds). Micronuclei can be a sign that chromosomes have broken into pieces, or that the cell has the wrong number of chromosomes [51]. Nucleoplasmic bridges point to problems with the mitotic spindle, the set of fibers that pulls chromosomes apart when a cell divides. Nuclear buds have been linked to the cell trying to repair damaged DNA [51,52].

Figure 4 shows the percentage of cells with each of these three signs of DNA damage, enlarged. When enlarged, the images look pixelated, meaning they are made of small squares. Sodium arsenite affected the genetic material of the cells. The high percentage of micronuclei shows that it caused chromosomes to break into pieces or the cells to end up with the wrong number of chromosomes (Figure 4a). Sodium arsenite also caused problems with how chromosomes are sorted out during division, which led to nucleoplasmic bridges (Figure 4b) and nuclear buds (Figure 4c). The silver nanoparticles did the same, but without significant differences (p > 0.05). In contrast, adding silver nanoparticles at 72 hours led to a significant drop (p < 0.05) in the number of micronuclei, nucleoplasmic bridges and nuclear buds. This suggests that this treatment reduces the DNA damage caused by sodium arsenite.
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion: What Our Results Mean

Our study points to a possible protective role for Argovit™ silver nanoparticles against the damage that sodium arsenite does to cells and their DNA in human lymphocytes grown in the lab. The protection was strongest when we gave the silver nanoparticles after the cells had already been exposed to the poison. We found no statistically significant differences in programmed cell death (apoptosis) between the groups. This means our study could not show a difference in cell death, though it does not prove there was none. Even so, our findings suggest that sodium arsenite mainly affects how cells multiply by disrupting the cell cycle, the regular series of steps a cell goes through to grow and divide. It seems to do this by stopping cells from dividing, rather than by killing them directly. The drop we saw in the nuclear division index (NDI), a measure of how many nuclei the cells had formed, shows that the cells had lost some of their ability to multiply. This fits with a pattern in which cells stop dividing (a cytostatic effect) rather than one in which they are killed (a cytotoxic effect) [53].

The lower NDI supports the idea that sodium arsenite holds back the cell cycle. It may do this by stopping cells at one of the checkpoints, the control points where a cell checks itself before moving on. These include the G1 checkpoint, before the cell starts copying its DNA, and the G2/M checkpoint, just before it divides [8,54]. When cells are held up like this, key signs of DNA damage may appear later or not at all. These signs include micronuclei (MNi), nucleoplasmic bridges (NPBs) and nuclear buds (NBuds), which are usually found in cells that are actively dividing. Other researchers have described this before. It fits the idea that when the cell cycle is blocked, tests of DNA damage can underestimate both the damage and the programmed cell death [51,55,56].

Our findings agree with earlier studies showing that a blocked cell cycle can make it harder to detect DNA damage. It can delay the appearance of visible signs of damage, and it can leave fewer cells available to examine. In addition, giving sodium arsenite together with silver nanoparticles seems to reduce the harm to cells, but it may not remove the risk of DNA damage [41,42]. This two-sided behavior suggests a subtle interaction between the two substances. The nanoparticles may help the cells' repair systems without completely preventing damage [57].

We found nucleoplasmic bridges in the group given arsenite only. This points to interference with the mitotic spindle, the set of fibers that pulls chromosomes apart during division, and with the proper separation of chromosomes. In contrast, the groups given silver nanoparticles showed no significant formation of these bridges. This suggests that the nanoparticles played a protective role, or at least had no effect, in this situation. In the same way, nuclear buds appeared in several groups. This suggests that the cells were actively repairing their DNA, and the silver nanoparticles may boost this repair, although that does not necessarily mean the damage was fully fixed [57,58].

In the group given Argovit™ silver nanoparticles after sodium arsenite, the nuclear division index was significantly higher than in the group given sodium arsenite alone (p < 0.05), as Figure 2a shows. This recovery suggests that the cells partly regained their ability to multiply, and that the arsenite's effect of stopping cells from dividing was weakened. At the same time, the same group showed a significant drop in the signs of DNA damage: micronuclei, nuclear buds and nucleoplasmic bridges (p < 0.05 for all three). This is in contrast to the higher levels caused by arsenite alone. These findings support the idea that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles not only reduce damage to cells but also reduce the instability of chromosomes and the abnormal nuclei that come with stress on the DNA [42].

The protective effect may be explained, at least in part, by the ability of silver nanoparticles to change how cells handle oxidative stress. Sodium arsenite is known to damage DNA by producing reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are harmful, highly reactive oxygen-based molecules. It also disrupts the formation of the mitotic spindle and encourages errors in chromosomes. At amounts too low to kill cells, Argovit™ silver nanoparticles may boost the cells' own antioxidant defenses, especially those that rely on glutathione (GSH), a natural substance in cells that neutralizes harmful oxygen-based molecules. Earlier studies by our group have shown that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles can stimulate responses that depend on glutathione. They may increase the activity of two enzymes, glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase, which are critical for neutralizing ROS and keeping the cell's chemical balance steady [42].

The surface of Argovit™ silver nanoparticles is coated with polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). This coating helps a biocorona, a layer of proteins, form when the particles meet proteins in blood serum, and this layer changes how the particles interact with cells [59,60,61,62]. The protein layer may reduce unwanted sticking, the way cells take up the particles, and the stress inside cells. This may add to the drop we saw in the signs of damage to cells and DNA [60,62]. The fewer nuclear buds and nucleoplasmic bridges may also reflect better DNA repair and proper separation of chromosomes. Taken together, these results suggest that giving Argovit™ silver nanoparticles after arsenite works against the damage arsenite does to cells and DNA. It may do this by strengthening antioxidant defenses, keeping the particles' behavior steady through the protein layer, and helping keep the cells' DNA intact [61].

Because our study used a longer, 144-hour culture, we took special care to reduce the problems that come with keeping cells in the lab for a long time. These include culture fatigue, where cells slowly lose their ability to grow and divide; replication stress, where copying the DNA becomes difficult; and DNA damage that happens on its own. To limit these effects, we replaced part of the culture liquid at 72, 96 and 120 hours. This kept nutrients available and stopped waste products from building up [59]. We also kept untreated control cultures under exactly the same conditions as the treated groups. These controls consistently showed low levels of micronuclei, programmed cell death and other nuclear abnormalities, which suggests there was little background damage. We also scored the cells in a blinded and randomized way, meaning the person scoring did not know which group each sample came from and the order was shuffled. This further supported the reliability of the effects we saw on cells and DNA. We did not use specific molecular markers of cell multiplication, of senescence (a state in which cells stop dividing for good) or of early DNA damage. Still, the design of the experiment and the consistent results in the controls make our findings easier to interpret in a long test like this one [59].

Another point to consider is how silver nanoparticles and sodium arsenite might interact physically and chemically. In our experiment, we gave sodium arsenite at 24 hours and the silver nanoparticles at 72 hours. Even so, some arsenite may have stayed in the culture liquid in a form that cells could still take up. It could then have reacted with the surfaces of the silver nanoparticles or with silver ions (Ag+) released from them. Such reactions may form compounds that contain both silver and arsenic, make substances stick to surfaces, or change the chemical forms the ions take. All of these could affect how much of each substance reaches the cells and how it acts. However, the PVP coating of Argovit™ silver nanoparticles likely changes how reactive their surface is and how they behave in liquid, and it may reduce direct reactions with arsenic and similar elements [62,63].

Still, under conditions such as low pH (more acidic) or oxidative stress, silver nanoparticles have been shown to take up, change or chemically alter metal and metalloid ions, including arsenic, both in the environment and in living things. We did not study these possible interactions in this work. They should be tested in future research using methods such as UV–Vis spectroscopy (which measures how a sample absorbs light), zeta potential analysis (which measures the electric charge on the particles' surface), inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (which measures very small amounts of elements) or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (which reveals the chemical state of elements at a surface). These methods would give useful insight into how the chemical forms change. They would also help show whether the protective effects of silver nanoparticles come from changes in the cells' biology, from the particles trapping the arsenic physically and chemically, or from both.

Extending the culture from 72 to 144 hours let us study two cell cycles, but it may also have added other factors. Longer exposure to nutrients such as PHA (a plant protein that triggers lymphocytes to start dividing) and to the poison, even with fresh culture liquid, may cause damage to cells and DNA that builds up over time. It may also lead to more cells stopping their division and possibly to senescence [64]. These effects could lower the nuclear division index and affect how we interpret the signs of multiplication and damage. On the other hand, a longer culture may give cells more chances to repair their DNA, though this would depend on how well the repair systems work and how severe the damage is [64].

Earlier studies by our group in living animals support these observations. In them, we tested whether Argovit™ silver nanoparticles could protect DNA in BALB/c mice, a common laboratory breed of mouse, exposed to well-known DNA-damaging cancer drugs. In one study [41], silver nanoparticles reduced the DNA damage caused by cyclophosphamide in red blood cells from the blood of the body. This showed up as fewer red blood cells with micronuclei at several time points after repeated exposure. In a more recent study [42], Argovit™ silver nanoparticles protected against the DNA damage caused by cytosine arabinoside (Ara-C). Again, the study followed the cells over time, which let us watch how damage built up and was repaired [41,42].

These findings confirm that the action of silver nanoparticles depends on time. They also strengthen the view that giving nanoparticles after treatment, as we did in our model of cells outside the body, may support recovery that happens later. Together, these studies give a solid basis for future lab tests with human lymphocytes that follow changes over time and look at each stage of the cell cycle separately. It is important to note that the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) test is a terminal-point test. It is designed to capture abnormal chromosomes and nuclei at the end of a set culture period. It cannot follow the cell cycle as it happens or show when the checkpoints switch on. In our study, the lower nuclear division index, together with no significant programmed cell death, fits with cells stopping their division, possibly because the cell cycle was disrupted. However, we cannot confirm that cells stopped at a particular stage, such as G1 or G2/M, without direct molecular evidence or measurements from instruments that track cells one by one.

Our laboratory does not currently have flow cytometry or cell sorting equipment, which are instruments that measure or sort cells one at a time. This limits our ability to include real-time markers of the cell cycle. Even so, we chose the longer CBMN test (144 hours) on purpose. It let us see the combined result of disrupted multiplication and unstable chromosomes over a period that matters biologically.

Future work may benefit from working with other research teams or from adding molecular tools that complement our approach. Examples include immunostaining, which uses antibodies to mark particular proteins, and RT-qPCR, which measures how active particular genes are. These could be used for key proteins that control the cell cycle, such as cyclins, p21 and Chk1/2. They would help confirm that the checkpoints are being used and help explain how Argovit™ silver nanoparticles protect cells. Meanwhile, the patterns we saw in the nuclear division index, nuclear buds and nucleoplasmic bridges offer useful insights into the delayed damage that sodium arsenite does to cells and DNA, and into how nanoparticles may reduce it [41,42].

A major strength of our study is that we adapted the CBMN test to a longer culture, which lets us see effects across two complete cell cycles [65]. This gives a fuller picture of delayed damage to cells and DNA. However, the longer culture also brings challenges, such as culture fatigue, running out of nutrients and more variation between results. These could affect how well cells survive and hide the effects of the treatments. Although silver nanoparticles showed a protective effect in reducing damage to cells, their role when combined with sodium arsenite seems complex, and under certain conditions they may even make DNA damage worse. This suggests that the safety of nanoparticles needs to be interpreted with care, especially when people are exposed to several substances at once.

Despite these limitations, it is important to note that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles have been tested widely, both in experiments and in medical use, and have shown a good safety record across many types of cells and many uses. Supporting evidence comes from earlier toxicity studies carried out under OECD Guideline 420, an international standard for testing how harmful a substance is. These studies reported that the amount of metallic silver needed to kill half of the test animals (the LD50) ranged from 1067 to 1806 mg/kg, meaning milligrams per kilogram of body weight. This places these products in Category 4 of the Globally Harmonized System, the international system for classifying how dangerous chemicals are [40]. When we consider the full product, including the PVP coating that keeps the particles stable, the LD50 is above 17,000 mg/kg. This puts Argovit™ in the "practically non-toxic" category.

Studies of tissue in mice found no significant tissue damage, and the silver nanoparticles built up only in the digestive tract [40]. Argovit™ has also shown no DNA damage in models of melanoma, a type of skin cancer [65], and it protected DNA against damage caused by cytosine arabinoside and cyclophosphamide in living animals [41,42]. Studies in the environment have reported little damage to cells and DNA in plant tests, such as those using the onion Allium cepa. This supports its safe use at low amounts in farming [15,66,67].

Argovit™ silver nanoparticles have also caused little bursting of human red blood cells, in blood from both healthy and diabetic donors, and little DNA damage in human lymphocytes [10,68]. Uses in medicine, including prevention of SARS-CoV-2 [69] and treatment of diabetic foot ulcers, further show that the product is well tolerated by the body [70,71]. Together, these findings show that Argovit™ silver nanoparticles have a large safety margin for both medical and environmental uses. This supports continuing to study them as possible ways to reduce DNA damage.
